                    ### Question
                    Luis is a 25-year-old boy who suffered splenectomy after a bicycle accident 1 year ago. He has a dog that bit him 24 hours ago and a small wound on his right hand. Go to your health center (located 3 hours from the nearest hospital) for fever of 39 º C, pain in the wound and malaise. On examination PA 100/60 mm Hg, HR 110 beats per minute, slight inflammation in the wound without pus. Which of the following actions is more indicated at this time?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Send to the hospital to vaccinate for rabies and tetanus and keep under observation.
opb. Clean the wound and administer intramuscular nonspecific gammaglobulin.
opc. Give 400 mg of oral moxifloxacin and send to the hospital.
opd. Give clindamycin 600 mg orally every 8 hours and observation.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Luis, an asplenic patient, is at increased risk of severe bacterial infections following a dog bite. Immediate antibiotic treatment is crucial due to his compromised immune status. Moxifloxacin is a broad-spectrum antibiotic effective against potential pathogens from dog bites, including Pasteurella multocida, which is particularly concerning in asplenic individuals. Therefore, administering 400 mg of oral moxifloxacin and sending him to the hospital is the most appropriate action. While rabies and tetanus vaccinations are important, the immediate risk of bacterial infection in an asplenic patient takes precedence. Clindamycin is not the first-line treatment for dog bites, and nonspecific gammaglobulin is not indicated in this scenario. The retrieved evidence paths about vaccination and rabies are not directly relevant to the immediate management of bacterial infection risk in this context.
